best_for: Chrome users who want ads and trackers blocked out of the box, keep their extensions, and do not want to manage an ad-blocker add-on.
description:
Brave is a web browser from Brave Software, an internet company that also runs its own search engine. Brave says more than 120 million people use it each month.

Most new installs start with Brave Search, which answers from Brave's own index of the web rather than Google's or Bing's, and Brave says it keeps no profile of you. The browser can hide YouTube ads, including the ones before and during videos, and it blocks cookie consent pop-ups too. It also moves pages to secure https where it can. If you want a leaner browser, Brave Origin is a paid edition that lets you remove extras such as News, Wallet and Web3 domains.

points.title: Blocking is on by default
points.text: Shields block third-party trackers and the ads that rely on them without setup. You can relax it per site, or turn on an aggressive mode that also hits first-party ads but can break some pages.

points.title: Brave's own ads are opt-in
points.text: Brave Rewards and its browser ads are off unless you join. Those who opt in earn BAT tokens for viewing them.

points.title: Some extras cost money
points.text: Brave Firewall + VPN is listed at USD 9.99 per month or USD 99.99 per year for up to 10 devices, with a 7-day trial; it has no Linux client yet. Leo, the built-in AI assistant, has a free tier with no account and a paid Premium tier. Prices were read on the date below.

points.title: Built on Chromium, minus Google
points.text: Brave is a Chromium fork with Google's account sync and Chrome telemetry removed, and it can import your Chrome settings on first run.

points.title: Linux: Brave prefers its own repos
points.text: Brave maintains the Flathub package listed here, and Flathub marks it verified, but Brave's Linux page says it does not yet work as well as the native packages and changes Chromium's sandbox. Brave recommends its apt, dnf and zypper repositories for 64-bit Intel and Arm.

points.title: Versions and installers
points.text: Windows has x86, x64 and Arm64 installers for one user or the whole machine, and the listing keeps 172 versions. Macs get Intel and Apple silicon builds for macOS 13 and later. macOS and Linux list only the current release.
